Seminar Title:

Computational Studies on Structure-Property Relations and Catalysis Based on Internal Electric Fields of Molecules and Oriented External Electric Fields as its Analog

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Chemistry

Speaker Name:

Lopita Swain ( Rollno : 521cy1018)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Chemistry Seminar Hall

Date and Time:

07 Oct 2026 11.30AM

Contact:

Rajeev R

Abstract:

Electric fields (EFs), both internal and external, emerge as versatile and decisive modulators of chemical reactivity, stereoselectivity, and catalytic efficiency across diverse reaction classes. This thesis systematically investigates their mechanistic influence through density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, revealing how intrinsic internal fields and applied external fields interact to control reactions. In Lewis acid mediated ring-closing carbonyl&ndasholefin metathesis and oxa-Diels&ndashAlder reactions, intermolecular fields arising from the Lewis acid augment conventional acidity, enhance ionic pseudo-pericyclic pathways, and function as directional vectors that catalyse or inhibit reactivity depending on orientation. The role of the internal EF in the P(III)/P(V) redox cycle is further elucidated. In phosphonamide-mediated deoxyfluorination, the neutral forms of the Ph3CF fluoride donor and Ar3B-shuttling catalyst preserve favourable charge separation and are stabilised by the internal field. In contrast, the charged forms (Ph3C+ and Ar3BF-) generate opposing fields that raise the reaction barriers. Internal EFs play a fundamental role by selectively stabilising transition states to bring catalysis and selectivity. External fields aligned with this intrinsic field reinforce stabilisation and lower activation energies antiparallel fields counteract it. Strain release in small-ring cycloalkane transformations, exemplified by the Rh(I)-catalysed [5+1] cycloaddition of vinylcyclopropane with CO, is synergistically enhanced by electric-field-induced alignment of the orbitals at the metal centre. A nonmonotonic catalytic response to an applied EF is observed in reactions involving nucleophile&ndashelectrophile (Nu&ndashEl) pairs. Any deviation in EF magnitude (decrease or increase) while maintaining constant field direction results in inhibition, and the corresponding threshold is termed the EF-phobic point. Generation of a metastable intermediate under higher EF is identified as the reason for EF-phobicity. EF-phobicity behavior is observed in NHC-catalyzed Stetter reactions, Nucleophile&ndashelectrophile C&ndashC bond-forming reactions, and hydride transfer reactions. The concept of EF-phobic reactivity extends to enzymatic systems where the internal EFs generated within enzymatic active sites have been examined and shown to lie within the catalytic regime of the EF effect.
